title: Benzyne: amination of 4-chlorotoluene
subtitle: Elimination to an aryne, then addition at either end

reactants.caption: 4-chlorotoluene + sodium amide (in liquid ammonia)
reactants.learnerPrompt: No nitro groups this time, and a very strong base. Draw what the amide ion does first.
hintTiers: Without electron-withdrawing groups, addition to the ring is far too slow. The amide ion (pKa of ammonia about 35) is a very strong base: which hydrogen is most acidic?

The hydrogen next to the chlorine is the most acidic one on the ring: chlorine pulls electrons from that carbon. The amide lone pair takes the drawn hydrogen, and the C–H pair stays on carbon as an aryl anion. Two arrows.
Amide N lone pair → new bond to the drawn H next to Cl; that C–H bond → a lone pair on its carbon.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: There is no nitro group to hold a negative charge, so addition to this ring is far too slow. The amide ion is a strong base: it takes a proton.
Chlorine is electron-rich. The amide ion takes a proton instead.

aryl-anion.caption: an aryl anion, with the lone pair next to the chlorine
aryl-anion.learnerPrompt: Chloride leaves. Draw how benzyne forms.
hintTiers: The lone pair sits in the ring plane, right beside the C–Cl bond. What can it push out?
The carbon lone pair forms a second π bond to the carbon bearing chlorine, and the C–Cl bond breaks onto chlorine. Two arrows.
Aryl anion lone pair → a π bond to the carbon bearing Cl; the C–Cl bond → a lone pair on chlorine.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Taking the proton back from ammonia only returns to the start. (It does happen: the deprotonation is reversible.) Let chloride leave.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Chloride does leave, but the carbon would have only two bonds. Use the lone pair next door to make a new π bond.

benzyne.caption: 4-methylbenzyne: a 'triple bond' in a six-membered ring

benzyne-and-amide.caption: 4-methylbenzyne + another amide ion
benzyne-and-amide.learnerPrompt: The amide ion adds to benzyne. Add it to the carbon that gives the amine where the chlorine was.
hintTiers: Benzyne's extra π bond lies in the ring plane, badly overlapped and strained: a powerful electrophile. Either end can be attacked.
The amide lone pair forms a bond to the carbon that carried chlorine, and the in-plane π pair moves onto the other carbon of the triple bond as a lone pair. Two arrows.
Amide N lone pair → new C–N bond to the carbon that carried Cl; the extra C≡C π bond → a lone pair on the other carbon.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Ammonia can add to benzyne too, but the amide ion is the far better nucleophile here. Use the amide ion.
That carbon is an ordinary aromatic CH. The reactive carbons are the two ends of the strained triple bond.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right carbon. It now has five bonds: move the in-plane π bond onto the other carbon.

para-anion.caption: aryl anion, amine para to the methyl group
para-anion.learnerPrompt: Ammonia, the solvent, protonates the aryl anion.
hintTiers: An aryl anion is a very strong base. Which species in the flask has an N–H proton to give?
The carbon lone pair takes the drawn hydrogen of ammonia, and the N–H pair stays on nitrogen. Two arrows.
Aryl anion lone pair → new C–H bond to the drawn H of ammonia; that N–H bond → a lone pair on nitrogen.

meta-anion.caption: aryl anion, amine meta to the methyl group
meta-anion.learnerPrompt: Ammonia, the solvent, protonates the aryl anion.
hintTiers: An aryl anion is a very strong base. Which species in the flask has an N–H proton to give?
The carbon lone pair takes the drawn hydrogen of ammonia, and the N–H pair stays on nitrogen. Two arrows.
Aryl anion lone pair → new C–H bond to the drawn H of ammonia; that N–H bond → a lone pair on nitrogen.

p-toluidine.caption: p-toluidine (4-methylaniline): the amine where the chlorine was

m-toluidine.caption: m-toluidine (3-methylaniline): the amine on the neighbouring carbon, formed in a similar amount

steps.explanationAfterStep: The amide ion removes the proton next to chlorine, whose pull on electrons makes it the most acidic ring hydrogen. The lone pair sits in an sp² orbital in the ring plane, not in the π system.
An elimination: benzyne forms. Its extra π bond is made from two sp² orbitals in the ring plane that barely overlap, so benzyne is extremely reactive and lives only briefly.
Also correct: proton and chloride leave in one E2-like step. Deuterium-labelling experiments show that the deprotonation is fast and reversible, so the two-step route is the textbook picture.

steps.caption: Sodium chloride is left out of the drawing. Sodium amide is used in excess: another amide ion meets the benzyne.

steps.explanationAfterStep: The amide ion adds to one end of the triple bond; the new lone pair again sits in the ring plane. The methyl group is far away and barely affects which end is attacked.
The amide ion is regenerated. The amine has ended up on the carbon that carried chlorine, para to the methyl group.
Also correct: the amide ion adds to the other end of the triple bond. Neither end is strongly favoured, so this route is just as important.
This gives m-toluidine: the amine is on the carbon next to where chlorine was (cine substitution). Labelling one ring carbon with ¹⁴C showed this kind of scrambling and proved the benzyne mechanism.

mechanismSummary: With no electron-withdrawing groups, SNAr is impossible. Instead the very strong base removes the proton next to chlorine, and chloride leaves: an elimination that gives benzyne, with a strained, in-plane extra π bond. An amide ion adds to either end of it and ammonia protonates the aryl anion. Attack at the carbon that carried chlorine gives p-toluidine; attack at its neighbour gives m-toluidine. Both form in similar amounts.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 22
